title: Literals
description: Write SQL values clearly using string, numeric, boolean, and NULL forms, with MySQL mode distinctions, apostrophe handling, typed comparisons, and explicit missing-value behavior.
notes:
## Values written directly into a statement

An SQL literal is a value represented directly in SQL text. A string such as a person's name, an unquoted numeric amount, and the NULL marker can appear in a statement for different purposes. Literals are distinct from identifiers, which name columns or tables. A query can return a literal without reading that value from any stored row.

This topic uses MySQL 8.4 for executable examples. Comparisons with standard SQL or another product are labeled because quoting, boolean representation, and conversion rules differ. The goal is to express the intended value clearly, not to rely on a permissive parser to guess what the author meant.

Consider a workshop registration table with registration_id, attendee_name, fee, and badge_note. The identifier distinguishes registrations, fee is an exact recorded amount, and badge_note is optional text. A missing note, an empty note, and the word NULL are three different possibilities. The SQL representation must preserve whichever of those facts the task actually requires.

## Writing character strings with single quotes

Use single quotes for string literals. A name containing an apostrophe needs a representation that does not accidentally end the string. Doubling an embedded single quote expresses that quote as part of the value. For example, the SQL literal for Nila O'Brien can be written with two adjacent apostrophes inside the quoted text.

```sql
SELECT 'Nila O''Brien' AS attendee_name;
```

The result contains one apostrophe in the name, not two. The doubled character belongs to SQL syntax; it does not change the person's stored spelling. A common error is to insert one unescaped apostrophe into hand-built SQL and then misread the resulting syntax failure as a database problem.

An empty string uses two enclosing single quotes with nothing between them. It is still a string value. A string containing a space is different from an empty string, and both differ from NULL under the MySQL model used here. Do not normalize those states into one value unless a stated product rule calls for that transformation.

## Separating string quoting from identifier quoting

A quoted name-like word can be data rather than an object reference. In standard SQL and PostgreSQL, double quotes delimit an identifier. MySQL normally also accepts double-quoted strings, but the ANSI_QUOTES mode changes their interpretation to identifiers. A copied example can therefore have different meaning under a different product or server mode.

For clear MySQL teaching examples, use single quotes for string values and backticks for identifiers when required. This keeps a constant such as the text students distinct from a table named students. The fact that a statement executes does not prove it selected the intended column; it may have returned the same constant on every row.

Backslash handling in MySQL also depends on SQL mode. The NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES mode changes whether backslash sequences act as escapes. Doubling an embedded quote avoids relying on backslash-based quote escaping in the examples here. For arbitrary application input, use the driver's supported parameter binding rather than attempting to reproduce every quoting and character-set rule manually.

## Keeping numbers numeric

Write an ordinary numeric literal without string quotes when the task requires a number. Forty-two written as digits is a numeric literal; the same digits inside single quotes form a character string. The distinction matters even when a particular comparison appears to convert one into the other automatically.

```sql
SELECT 42 AS numeric_value, '42' AS text_value;
```

A client may display both results similarly, but appearance is not a complete type description. When a numeric column is compared with a quoted numeric-looking string, MySQL can apply implicit conversion under its comparison rules. Other contexts or products may behave differently. Match values to their intended types rather than assuming every successful implicit conversion is harmless.

Invalid numeric text is especially risky. A value such as forty-two written as letters is not an ordinary numeric literal. Do not count on permissive conversion to produce a meaningful number or on every context to reject it identically. Validate untrusted input at the appropriate boundary and use an explicit supported conversion only when its failure behavior is understood.

## Choosing exact measurements and boundaries

A decimal amount such as 125.50 should be understood in the context of its database type and unit. For fee examples, an exact decimal column communicates the intended monetary representation more clearly than an unexplained approximate measurement. A literal alone does not establish currency, precision requirements, or authority to change financial data.

Boundary conditions should use the required comparison explicitly. A filter for fee greater than or equal to one hundred includes exactly one hundred. Greater than one hundred does not. A string comparison on text that happens to contain digits can have different ordering from a numeric comparison, so the table's type and literal form both matter.

Do not infer index performance from quoting alone. Implicit conversion can complicate semantics and access choices, but the actual plan depends on the expression, types, indexes, and engine. Explain the correctness risk first and use plan evidence for performance claims. A universal statement that every quoted numeric value disables every index would be inaccurate.

## Representing and comparing absence

NULL represents a missing or unknown value under the modeled meaning of the column. It is not the character string NULL and not the number zero. In the registration example, NULL badge_note means no note has been recorded. An empty note is a recorded empty string, while the quoted text NULL is literally four letters.

Use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL to test for absence. Equality with NULL does not produce the ordinary true comparison needed to select missing values. A WHERE clause retains rows whose condition is true, so fee equals NULL is not the right way to find missing fees. The same distinction matters in combined conditions and output mappings.

When displaying notes, a CASE expression can label the missing state while preserving recorded values. If the task also needs to distinguish an empty string, test that state separately. Replacing every missing value with an empty string may simplify formatting but erases information about whether any value was recorded.

## Understanding boolean and date-related forms

MySQL recognizes TRUE and FALSE as boolean-value forms associated with one and zero. This does not imply that every product has the same boolean storage type or accepts the same expressions. PostgreSQL has a native boolean type, while SQL Server commonly uses bit for stored two-state values. A cross-dialect example needs an explicit target rather than a generic promise of identical behavior.

Date and timestamp values also need type-aware handling. A date-looking string does not by itself prove that a stored column has a date type or that every product interprets it the same way. Use the selected database's documented representation and avoid ambiguous local formats. Detailed date operations belong to their dedicated topic; here the key distinction is between text appearance and typed meaning.

Literal spelling is only one side of expression behavior. The receiving column type, operator, SQL mode, and relevant comparison rules help determine the result. Test representative values in the intended engine before claiming that a statement is portable or that a displayed output establishes identical types.

## Moving from examples to application input

Handwritten literals are useful for learning and reproducible fixtures. Application requests should normally pass values separately through the established driver API. This handles apostrophes and other characters as data without making the application assemble unsafe statement fragments. Parameter binding still needs trusted validation and authorization around the operation.

Check examples with an apostrophe, an empty string, NULL, the literal text NULL, a zero fee, and a threshold fee. Compare the actual output with the task's meaning, including required ordering. These cases make literals a precise part of SQL reasoning: the written value, its type context, and the absence policy must agree before a query can be called correct.

references.title: MySQL string literals and SQL modes

questions.question_text: In standard SQL, what character delimits a string literal?
options: Double quotes
Single quotes
Backticks
Square brackets
questions.explanation: Standard SQL uses single quotes for string literals; double quotes delimit identifiers.

questions.question_text: How do you correctly represent an apostrophe inside a single-quoted string literal, e.g. for the name O'Brien?
options: 'O\\'Brien'
'O'Brien'
'O''Brien' (doubling the apostrophe)
It cannot be done — apostrophes are forbidden in string literals
questions.explanation: Standard SQL escapes an embedded single quote by doubling it: 'O''Brien'.

questions.question_text: In standard SQL and PostgreSQL, what does `"students"` (double-quoted) refer to?
options: The string value 'students'
An identifier literally named students (e.g. a table or column)
A syntax error in every dialect
A comment
questions.explanation: Double quotes delimit identifiers in standard SQL/PostgreSQL — this is a common trap for people used to MySQL's default double-quoted strings.

questions.question_text: Should a numeric literal like 42 normally be quoted?
options: Yes, always, in every dialect
No — quoting it turns it into a string literal instead of a number
Only on Sundays
Only in SELECT statements, never in WHERE
questions.explanation: Numeric literals are unquoted; wrapping a number in quotes makes it a string literal, which is a different type.

questions.question_text: Which of these is TRUE about boolean literals across dialects?
options: Every SQL dialect has an identical native boolean type and TRUE/FALSE literal
PostgreSQL and MySQL support TRUE/FALSE, but SQL Server has no true boolean type and commonly uses 1/0 instead
Boolean literals do not exist in any SQL dialect
TRUE and FALSE are reserved words that cannot appear in any query
questions.explanation: MySQL recognizes TRUE/FALSE as 1/0; PostgreSQL has a native boolean type, while SQL Server commonly uses bit. Storage and expressions are dialect-specific.

questions.question_text: Why is MySQL's default acceptance of double-quoted strings ("Asha") considered a dialect quirk rather than standard behavior?
options: Because it isn't actually supported by MySQL at all
Because in the SQL standard and other engines like PostgreSQL, double quotes mean an identifier, not a string, so the same syntax means different things elsewhere
Because double quotes are illegal characters in SQL entirely
Because MySQL requires triple quotes for strings
questions.explanation: MySQL can accept double-quoted strings unless ANSI_QUOTES makes double quotes delimit identifiers; single quotes are the clear string form.

questions.question_text: What is the most accurate description of NULL as a literal?
options: NULL behaves exactly like any other literal value in comparisons
NULL represents an unknown/absent value and needs its own special comparison rules, unlike ordinary literals
NULL is simply a synonym for the number zero
NULL is only valid inside string columns
questions.explanation: NULL is fundamentally different from other literals — it participates in three-valued logic rather than ordinary equality comparison.

questions.question_text: In MySQL, an integer fee column is compared with the quoted text value '100'. What should a reviewer recognize?
options: The query always fails outright with a fatal type error
Implicit conversion may occur; use a type-appropriate value and verify semantics and plans rather than assuming identical behavior everywhere
The comparison always silently returns zero rows regardless of data
String and integer literals are indistinguishable in SQL
questions.explanation: Successful conversion does not prove portability or a particular index outcome. Actual types and expressions determine behavior.

questions.question_text: Which three values are distinct in the MySQL registration example?
options: NULL, no value, and unknown are always three stored types
NULL, an empty string, and the string NULL
Zero, 0, and numeric zero are three different amounts
Every quoted and unquoted token means the same thing
questions.explanation: Absence, recorded empty text, and four recorded letters have different meanings.

questions.question_text: What does doubling an apostrophe inside a single-quoted literal represent?
options: Two stored apostrophes in every case
The end of the database transaction
One apostrophe in the resulting string
A quoted column name
questions.explanation: The doubled quote is literal syntax, not an extra character in the intended value.

questions.question_text: What value does 'Nila O''Brien' represent?
options: Nila OBrien
Nila O''Brien
Nila O'Brien
attendee_name
questions.explanation: Two adjacent embedded quotes encode one apostrophe.

questions.question_text: Which predicate finds registrations whose badge_note is absent?
options: badge_note = 'NULL'
badge_note = NULL
badge_note = ''
badge_note IS NULL
questions.explanation: IS NULL tests absence rather than a recorded string or unknown equality.

questions.question_text: A badge_note contains the actual text 'NULL'. Does badge_note IS NULL match it?
options: No; it is a recorded string
Yes; those four letters always mean absence
Only if the fee is zero
Only if the identifier is quoted
questions.explanation: The text NULL is not the NULL marker.

questions.question_text: A fee of exactly 100 must qualify. Which numeric condition expresses the inclusive threshold?
options: fee > 100
fee = 'at least one hundred'
fee IS NULL
questions.explanation: The inclusive comparison retains the boundary value.

questions.question_text: ANSI_QUOTES is enabled and a query uses double quotes around a word. What interpretation applies?
options: Always ordinary string quoting
Automatic integer conversion
Identifier quoting
Transaction rollback
questions.explanation: The mode changes double-quote meaning; use single quotes for strings.

questions.question_text: A server changes backslash-escape behavior through NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES. What should copied examples avoid assuming?
options: That doubled apostrophes represent quoted text
That values can be bound through a driver
That identifiers and literals are different roles
That backslash quote escapes behave the same under every mode
questions.explanation: SQL modes are part of the execution context.

questions.question_text: A client displays 42 and '42' similarly. What is not proved by their appearance?
options: That their SQL representations and type contexts are identical
That both can appear in a SELECT
That the client produced output
That the characters look alike
questions.explanation: Display formatting alone does not establish type equivalence.

questions.question_text: An application receives a name containing an apostrophe. Which approach should it normally use?
options: Concatenate it directly into SQL
Pass the name through the established driver's parameter binding
Remove every apostrophe from the user's name
Treat the name as an identifier
questions.explanation: Values should remain data; manual ad hoc escaping is not a substitute for the supported binding API.

questions.question_text: A report maps both NULL and an empty note to the same blank display. Which question must review answer?
options: Whether the index name is uppercase
Whether all row IDs are equal
Whether losing the missing-versus-recorded-empty distinction is intended
Whether the table has no primary key
questions.explanation: A formatting simplification can erase information the task needs.

questions.question_text: A quoted numeric comparison executes successfully. What should not be claimed without further evidence?
options: That this execution completed
That SQL can compare expressions
That a result was observed
That every engine, type context, and access plan behaves identically
questions.explanation: Successful execution establishes neither universal portability nor an exact plan.

coding_problems.title: Find an attendee whose name contains an apostrophe
coding_problems.task: Return registration_id and attendee_name for rows whose attendee_name equals Nila O'Brien. Write the string literal with a doubled apostrophe and order by registration_id. Do not alter or remove the apostrophe from the data.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE registrations (registration_id INT PRIMARY KEY, attendee_name VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL, fee DECIMAL(8,2) NULL CHECK (fee >= 0), badge_note VARCHAR(40) NULL);
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO registrations VALUES (2,'Nila O''Brien',100.00,NULL),(1,'Nila OBrien',100.00,NULL),(3,'Nila O''Brien',0.00,'');
coding_problems.expected:
registration_id	attendee_name
2	Nila O'Brien
3	Nila O'Brien
constraints: Different registrations can have the same attendee_name
Fixtures use identical letter case for the matching names
edge_cases: Do not match the spelling without an apostrophe
An absent match returns no rows
hints: Compare the name field to a string value
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT registration_id, attendee_name FROM registrations WHERE attendee_name = 'Nila O''Brien' ORDER BY registration_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The doubled quote creates one apostrophe in the comparison value. The query preserves separate registrations with that name.

coding_problems.title: Filter exact fees and classify note values
coding_problems.task: For registrations with fee >= 100, return registration_id, fee, note_state. Use 'missing' for a NULL badge_note, 'empty' for an empty string, 'literal null text' for the exact uppercase string NULL, and 'other text' otherwise. Use a binary comparison for note text so letter case and spaces are not folded by collation rules. Preserve the distinction between no fee and zero fee. Order by registration_id.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE registrations (registration_id INT PRIMARY KEY, attendee_name VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL, fee DECIMAL(8,2) NULL CHECK (fee >= 0), badge_note VARCHAR(40) NULL);
coding_problems.expected:
registration_id	fee	note_state
1	100.00	missing
2	125.50	empty
3	100.00	literal null text
4	100.00	other text
constraints: Fees are exact decimals or NULL
Note classification is case-sensitive and distinguishes spaces
edge_cases: NULL note differs from empty and the letters NULL
A single-space note is other text
hints: Use IS NULL before ordinary string tests
Use CAST(badge_note AS BINARY) for exact note comparisons
Use unquoted numeric 100 for the fee boundary
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT registration_id, fee, CASE WHEN badge_note IS NULL THEN 'missing' WHEN CAST(badge_note AS BINARY) = '' THEN 'empty' WHEN CAST(badge_note AS BINARY) = 'NULL' THEN 'literal null text' ELSE 'other text' END AS note_state FROM registrations WHERE fee >= 100 ORDER BY registration_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The numeric filter includes the boundary and excludes unknown fees. CASE handles absence separately, and binary string comparison prevents case or space folding from merging distinct recorded text.

validation_cases.expected:
registration_id	fee	note_state
1	100.00	other text
2	100.00	other text
